```csharp
        .Reads(viewProj)
        .Writes(hdr)
        .WritesDepth(depth)
        .Draw(scene, static (ctx, scene) =>
        {
            // Your own draw list, however you build it — scene.VisibleObjects is read live each frame.
            foreach (var obj in scene.VisibleObjects)
            {
                var call = DrawCall.Create(obj.Mesh, "scene");
                call.Material = obj.Material;          // fills the technique's reflected sampler slots
                // The per-draw block matching the shader. `ref` because the bytes alias this storage until the
                // draw is submitted — passing a temporary would leave the engine reading a dead local, so the
                // compiler rejects it rather than letting it corrupt at runtime.
                var model = obj.ModelMatrix;
                call.SetUniforms(ref model);
                ctx.Draw(call);
            }
        });

    // Tonemap pass: sample HDR, write the swapchain. `hdr` is a build-time resource handle (not
    // per-frame data), so capturing it directly is fine — only per-frame values need the state overload.
    g.Pass("tonemap")
        .Samples(hdr)
        .Writes(g.Backbuffer)
        .Draw(ctx => ctx.FullScreen("tonemap", hdr));

    // The terminal: present the swapchain. Acquire/present sync is derived behind this.
    g.Present(g.Backbuffer);
});

engine.SetGraph(graph);
```

The pass-builder verbs are the whole scheduling vocabulary — `.Writes` (produce a colour target), `.Blends` (accumulate onto existing contents), `.Samples` (bind as a shader-read input), `.WritesDepth` / `.ReadsDepth`, `.ReadWrites` (compute storage), `.ReadsVertex` (a vertex/instance stream), and `.Reads` (a constants or storage buffer). From these the engine derives execution order, every barrier, and every layout transition.

### 4. Render loop

`FrameInputs` carries only `DeltaSeconds` and `Time` (both `double`) — there is no engine `Camera` or `Scene`. View, light, and time data flow in through the neutral channels your passes read: write them by handle each frame *before* `Render`. Driven by Silk.NET's render callback:

```csharp
var elapsed = 0.0;   // double: an accumulator kept as float loses precision over a long session

window.Render += delta =>
{
    elapsed += delta;

    // Publish the matrix the "scene" pass reads. (Loom.Concepts.Camera folds in the
    // clip-space correction so the same matrix is correct on both backends.)
    engine.Write(viewProj, camera.ViewProjection);

    engine.Render(new FrameInputs
    {
        DeltaSeconds = delta,    // double, seconds since the previous frame
        Time         = elapsed,  // double, seconds since startup
    });
};

window.Run();        // blocks, calling Render until the window closes
engine.WaitIdle();   // drain the GPU before teardown
```

Because the graph captures only the stable `viewProj` handle, `engine.Write` updates the bytes the shader reads without rebuilding the graph. The same immutable `RenderGraph` drives every frame; only a structural change (different passes, resources, or domains) triggers a rebake.

## Loading assets

`Loom.Assets` provides neutral, graphics-API-free loaders that produce engine-boundary types (`TextureData`, `Vertex[]`). Hand those to the engine to mint stable `Texture`, `Mesh`, and `Material` handles, each living for the engine's lifetime.

**Images → textures → materials.** `ImageLoader.Load` decodes a PNG/JPG to `TextureData` (with a CPU-generated mip chain); pass `TextureFormat.Rgba8Srgb` for colour/albedo or `TextureFormat.Rgba8Unorm` for data such as normal maps. `CreateMaterial` bundles textures in the order the technique's shader binds them:

```csharp
using Loom.Assets;
using Loom.Core.Materials;

var albedoData = ImageLoader.Load("textures/albedo.png", TextureFormat.Rgba8Srgb);
var normalData = ImageLoader.Load("textures/normal.png", TextureFormat.Rgba8Unorm);

var albedo = engine.CreateTexture(albedoData);
var normal = engine.CreateTexture(normalData);

var material = engine.CreateMaterial(albedo, normal);   // texture 0 → sampler slot 0, …
```

**glTF → meshes.** `GltfLoader.Load` walks the node graph, bakes world transforms, and flattens the model to drawable primitives. Each `ModelPrimitive` carries `Vertices` (Loom's canonical position/normal/uv/tangent `Vertex`) and `Indices`, ready for `CreateMesh`:

```csharp
var model = GltfLoader.Load("models/character.glb");

foreach (var prim in model.Primitives)
{
    var mesh = engine.CreateMesh(prim.Vertices, prim.Indices);
    // … pair the mesh with a material and add it to your draw list …
}
```

For a rigged model, `model.Skeleton` and `model.Clips` carry the skeleton and animation clips, and a primitive's `SkinnedVertices` feed `engine.CreateSkinnedMesh(prim.SkinnedVertices, prim.Indices)` for the GPU pre-skin path (`ctx.DispatchSkin`). HDR environment maps load with `ImageLoader.LoadHdr`, which returns `Rgba16F` `TextureData`.

---

# Shader authoring

The Slang-side contract: what a shader must declare so Loom's backends can bind it, and why the rules are what they are.

[`api-vocabulary.md`](api-vocabulary.md) documents the C# surface. This is the other half — the part written in `.slang` — and until now it lived only in backend source comments, which is a poor place for a contract app authors have to satisfy.

One source compiles to **SPIR-V** (Vulkan), **signed DXIL** (DirectX 12), and **WGSL** (WebGPU). The targets number their bindings differently, so a shader numbers none of them: Slang does, per target, and each backend binds by what that target's reflection says (§2). What the targets still disagree about is quarantined in one file — `Loom.Shaders/Shaders/loom_platform.module.slang` — behind macros.

---

## 1. The platform macros

`#include "loom_platform.module.slang"` first, then use these instead of writing a target conditional yourself.

| Macro | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `LOOM_PUSH_CONSTANT` | Marks the small inline scalar block. `[[vk::push_constant]]` for SPIR-V/DXIL; lowers to an ordinary `uniform` for WGSL, which has no push constants. |
| `LOOM_FULLSCREEN_POS(uv)` | Clip position for a fullscreen triangle fabricated from `SV_VertexID`, given its 0..2 uv. |
| `LOOM_CLIP_POS(xy)` | Clip position for geometry already authored in NDC (−1..1) — the same job as above for a shader that isn't fullscreen-shaped. |
| `LOOM_OVERLAY_POS(px, scale, translate)` | Clip position for a 2D overlay/UI vertex in surface pixels. |
| `LOOM_CLIP_TO_UV(clip)` | Screen uv (0..1, top-left origin) of a clip-space position, for reprojecting a world point to sample a G-buffer there. |

The four position macros all exist for one reason: **NDC-Y**. Vulkan and DirectX 12 present a Y-down NDC (DX12 via a negative-height viewport), WebGPU a Y-up one with no negative viewport. A shader that goes through the camera never notices, because `Camera.ViewProjection` composes `IEngineClipSpace.ClipSpaceCorrection`. A shader that writes clip space *directly* has no camera to carry that correction, so the convention has to be applied at the point of emission — which is what these macros do.

> **Invariant:** `loom_platform.module.slang` is the only shader in the repository containing an `#ifdef LOOM_WGSL`. If you find yourself writing one, the macro you need is missing — add it there rather than branching in place. `grep -rl LOOM_WGSL --include=*.slang` should return exactly that one file.

---

## 2. Declaration order is the only numbering

A shader declares its resources and gives them no numbers:

```hlsl
Sampler2D albedoTex;
ConstantBuffer<ViewProj> view;
ConstantBuffer<PerDraw>  draw;
```

Slang numbers them for each target in declaration order: SPIR-V bindings in one list, D3D registers per kind (`t`, `s`, `b` and `u` counted apart, a `Sampler2D` taking a `t` and an `s`), WGSL bindings in one list (a `Sampler2D` taking two). Every stage of a module gets the same numbers. The build writes each target's numbers to its own reflection sidecar, and each backend binds by its own:

| Target | Sidecar | The backend binds |
|---|---|---|
| SPIR-V | `<name>.json` | each descriptor at its reflected binding (§3) |
| DXIL | `<name>.dxil.json` | each root parameter at its reflected register (§4) |
| WGSL | `<name>.wgsl.json` | each bind-group entry at its reflected binding (§6) |

What a shader does state is **order**. A pass's inputs fill a technique's slots kind by kind in declaration order: its `k`-th sampled input goes to the `k`-th `Sampler2D` declared, its `k`-th storage buffer to the `k`-th buffer, and its uniform slots are filled as §5 says. So a module that every lit shader includes declares its resources before the shader's own, and they come first in every pass that draws with it.

Don't write `[[vk::binding]]` or `: register(...)` yourself. They buy nothing, since every backend binds by whatever its reflection reports, and a register survives into the WGSL compile, where it becomes that parameter's WGSL binding (warning 39029) and registers of different kinds (`b1` and `t1`) collide.

---

## 3. Vulkan: one descriptor set, at reflected bindings

Everything lands in **set 0**, and `VulkanTechnique.CreateSetLayout` builds one entry per parameter **at the binding reflection gives it**, with the descriptor type its reflected shape implies and a descriptor count from its reflected slot span.

**No two parameters may claim the same slot** — an arrayed binding claims all of its. `ShaderLayoutParityTests` asserts it over every shipped sidecar, so a collision fails the suite rather than the picture.

---

## 4. DirectX 12: a root signature at reflected registers

The root signature is, in order: an optional 32-bit root-constants block, then one root CBV per reflected constant buffer, then an optional SRV descriptor table with a static sampler per sampled input, then any storage-buffer root SRVs (a compute technique's read-write storage goes in a UAV table, or a root UAV for a raw buffer). Each is built at the register the DXIL sidecar gives its parameter (`DirectX12Registers`), one descriptor range per texture, so the registers need not be contiguous.

The root-constants block is the shader's `LOOM_PUSH_CONSTANT` block, which D3D lays out as an ordinary constant buffer in declaration order: the backend finds it as the one constant buffer the SPIR-V sidecar doesn't list as a descriptor. A technique with root constants and no push block puts them after the shader's last constant buffer, where they overlap nothing.

---

## 5. Uniform slots are filled in a defined order

A technique's uniform buffers are filled, slot 0 upward:

1. the slot reflection identifies as the **per-material parameter block**, if the shader declares one (§7)
2. then the pass's `.Reads(...)` constants, **in declaration order**
3. then the per-draw block (`DrawCall.Uniforms` / `SetUniforms`)

So a pass declaring `.Reads(viewProj)` and a draw supplying a per-draw block gives the shader two constant buffers, view-projection first. Adding a second `.Reads` inserts it before the per-draw block — the per-draw block is always last.

A compute dispatch fills its constant buffers from the pass's `.Reads(...)` alone, in declaration order: it has no per-draw block, and its push rides only the scalar block (§9), never a uniform slot. On DirectX 12 they are root CBVs as a draw's are. A compute technique that declares more constant buffers than its pass reads throws at dispatch on every backend, rather than dispatching with a slot unbound. The Particles demo's fountain (`particle_fountain.slang`) reads its shape this way.

A compute technique reads app-written storage the same way: each read-only `StructuredBuffer<T>` it declares takes the pass's `.Reads(storage)` in declaration order, while each `RWStructuredBuffer<T>` takes the dispatch's own storage. Declare the read-write buffers first and the read-only after them. A compute technique declaring more read-only buffers than its pass reads throws at dispatch on every backend, as does a dispatch supplying a different number of read-write buffers, or of storage images, than the technique declares: a surplus would be bound nowhere, a shortfall would leave a slot unbound. The Storage Scatter demo (`storage_scatter.slang`) expands a density map written once into a field of sparks this way.

A read-only `StructuredBuffer<T>` in a compute technique binds **only** the pass's `.Reads` storage (`g.Storage`). A buffer the GPU produced (`g.Buffer`, written by an earlier dispatch) reaches a dispatch only through its own storage list, which fills the `RWStructuredBuffer<T>` slots, so declare it `RWStructuredBuffer<T>` even where the shader only reads it.

The binding is **positional, never by name**, for draws and dispatches alike: a technique's `k`-th storage buffer (in binding order; a compute technique's `k`-th read-only one) takes the `k`-th storage buffer its pass `.Reads`. A technique that reads only some of a pass's buffers must declare them in the order the pass reads them, from its first: one declaring only the pass's second gets its first. Each slot's reflected element size is held to the size of the buffer it lands on (the `T` of `g.Storage<T>`, packed or padded to the element's std430 alignment), and a mismatch throws at the draw or dispatch naming both, which catches that mistake wherever the two element types differ in size.

---

## 6. WebGPU: bind groups from the WGSL

Slang assigns WGSL bindings in declaration order, a combined `Sampler2D` taking **two** (texture + sampler), and the WebGPU backend recovers the real assignments from the emitted WGSL and its sidecar.

The three sidecars are *different index spaces for the same source*. A `ShaderReflection` records which one it holds, and building a Vulkan or DirectX 12 layout from a WGSL reflection throws rather than producing a layout that looks plausible and binds the wrong things.

Consequences worth knowing: WGSL has no push constants (`LOOM_PUSH_CONSTANT` becomes a uniform), and vertex-input locations may be permuted relative to stream order, which is why the backend parses them rather than assuming.

---

## 7. The per-material parameter block

A shader opts into per-material parameters by declaring a constant buffer under the reserved name **`loomMaterial`**:

```hlsl
struct LoomMaterial
{
    float4 baseColor;
    float4 emissive;
    float4 metallicRoughness;
};

ConstantBuffer<LoomMaterial> loomMaterial;
```

Reflection reports which uniform slot it is and how many bytes it occupies; the engine stages a material's bytes into that slot on every draw using it. Convention is to declare it last, but nothing depends on that — it binds at whatever slot reflection reports.

**Lay the struct out in 16-byte-aligned rows.** HLSL constant-buffer packing and WGSL uniform layout agree on `float4` and disagree on tighter shapes, so a bare `float3` or a trailing `float` lands at different offsets on different backends. Pack loose scalars into a `float4` instead.

The engine has no opinion about what the bytes mean — `GltfMaterialFactors` in `Loom.Assets` is one possible shape, not a privileged one.

---

## 8. Entry points

Name them `vertexMain` / `fragmentMain` / `computeMain` and mark them with `[shader("vertex")]`, `[shader("fragment")]`, `[shader("compute")]`. The build detects the stages from those attributes; the SDK errors if a declared entry name isn't found.

A compute technique states its entry once via `TechniqueDescriptor.Compute("shader")`. What the compiled artifact ends up calling that entry internally is the backend's problem — Vulkan resolves the real SPIR-V entry from the module, so a toolchain that renames the sole entry to `main` is handled without the author knowing.

**Variants.** One source compiled again with macros defined, under a name of its own, is a `LoomSlangVariant`, not a second file that defines the macro and includes the first:

```xml
<ItemGroup>
  <LoomSlangVariant Include="Shaders\terrain.slang;Shaders\car.slang" Suffix="_cast" Defines="CAST" />
</ItemGroup>
```

That makes `terrain_cast` and `car_cast` beside `terrain` and `car`, on every backend, each a shader of its own that a `TechniqueDescriptor` names (`Defines` takes a list, `A;B=2`). The stages are found by scanning the source, as an entry's are, and the scan doesn't see `#ifdef`: a variant that compiles a stage out names the stages it keeps with `Stages="vertex"` on the item. Declare variants before the SDK's targets are imported, so the IDE's up-to-date check sees their outputs.

---

## 9. Where scalar parameters actually go

`ctx.FullScreen(technique, push, …)` and `ctx.Dispatch(technique, groups, push, …)` take a `ReadOnlySpan<float>`. Where it lands depends on what the technique declared:

| The shader declares | The span goes to | Bound |
|---|---|---|
| `LOOM_PUSH_CONSTANT` block (`HasFragmentPush: true`) | push constants / root constants | **16 floats** — the block's fixed size |
| a descriptor-bound `ConstantBuffer<T>` instead | the next free uniform slot, via the per-frame ring | **that buffer's declared size** (CSM's is 68 floats wide, and it pushes 68) |

A technique has one or the other, so the same bytes are offered to both channels and the technique's binding model takes whichever it declares.

The uniform route is not uncapped: it is a real buffer, but a buffer of the size the shader declared, and reflection reports that size. Pushing more than the target holds is an error, on either route — as is pushing when the technique declares no block *and* the pass's `.Reads` have already filled every constant buffer it reflects, which leaves the bytes nowhere to go. All three cases used to be silent (truncated, or dropped entirely); they now throw `TechniqueMismatchException` naming the pass, the technique, and both counts.

One thing the check cannot do: a constant buffer's reflected size includes padding to its 16-byte rows, so a push that *fits* is not thereby laid out the way the shader reads it. Getting the size right does not excuse §7's advice about packing loose scalars into a `float4`.

---

# Loom Effect Cookbook

Reference patterns for the shipped rendering effects. Each entry shows the resource topology and the key graph structure in current API. These are *application-side* recipes: they add ordinary passes that name app-supplied shaders, declare their reads and writes, and let the engine derive the ordering, every barrier and layout transition, and transient-memory aliasing. Nothing here is privileged engine vocabulary.

The shapes below are taken from the live demos in [`Loom.Gallery/Demos/`](../Loom.Gallery/Demos) — read those for the complete implementations (shader bodies, per-frame data, ImGui knobs).

A few conventions used throughout:

- A graph is authored once with `RenderGraph.Define(g => { … })`; passes chain their verbs — `g.Pass("name").Writes(x).Samples(y).Draw(ctx => …)` — and a compute pass is `g.Compute("name").ReadWrites(b).Dispatch(ctx => …)`.
- `g.Present(handle)` and `g.Readback(handle)` are **graph-builder** methods, not pass verbs.
- Targets are allocated on a `Domain`: `g.Screen.Color("name", Format.X)` (native size), `domain.Color("name", Format.X)`, `domain.Depth("name", Format.Depth32F)`, or a fractional mip with `domain.Color("name", Format.X, scale: 0.5f)`. `g.Backbuffer` is the swapchain target.
- `.Draw` bodies are elided with `…` where the body is incidental; the **graph structure** — passes, verbs, handles, formats — is real.

---

## Deferred G-buffer + lighting

Classic deferred shading. The geometry pass writes a packed G-buffer (albedo + world normal + world position, plus depth) as a multiple-render-target write; a single fullscreen lighting pass samples those targets and produces the lit HDR colour. Lighting accumulates inside the shader — the per-frame light/sun data rides the fragment push (or a constants channel) the pass reads.

```
scene ─► gbuffer { albedo, normal, position, depth }
                          │  .Samples(albedo, normal, position)
                ┌─────────▼──────────┐
                │  lighting           │
                │  (fullscreen)       │
                └─────────────────────┘
                          │
                       lit (HDR)
```

```csharp
var albedo   = g.Screen.Color("albedo",   Format.Rgba8Srgb);
var normal   = g.Screen.Color("normal",   Format.Rgba16F);
var position = g.Screen.Color("position", Format.Rgba16F);
var depth    = g.Screen.Depth("depth",    Format.Depth32F);
var lit      = g.Screen.Color("lit",      Format.Rgba16F);

g.Pass("gbuffer")
    .Reads(viewProj)
    .Writes(albedo, normal, position)   // multiple .Writes targets = MRT
    .WritesDepth(depth)
    .Draw(ctx => { /* draw scene meshes with the "gbuffer" technique */ });

g.Pass("lighting")
    .Samples(albedo, normal, position)
    .Writes(lit)
    .Draw(ctx => ctx.FullScreen("lighting", albedo, normal, position));
```

Notes:

- Multiple `.Writes` on one pass is the MRT idiom — the engine packs them as the pass's colour attachments in order, and `ctx.FullScreen` binds the lighting pass's `.Samples` inputs in the same order they're declared.
- **Many lights** can be folded into the single fullscreen pass (a light loop in the shader), or layered as additive light volumes — see [2D normal-mapped lights](#forward-alpha-blend-transparency) for the `.Blends`-accumulate variant.

---

## Single shadow map (+ cascaded)

A depth-only pass renders the casters from the *sun's* view into a shadow map that lives in its own square domain; the lighting pass samples that depth map and compares against each pixel's projected sun-space depth. The shadow pass reads the sun's view-projection; the G-buffer pass reads the camera's — the deferred split is what lets each transform be a single published matrix.

```
            sun view                       camera view
                │                               │
   ┌────────────▼───────────┐    ┌──────────────▼───────────┐
   │ shadow (depth-only)     │    │ gbuffer (MRT + depth)    │
   │  .WritesDepth(shadowMap)│    │  .Writes(albedo, normal,…)│
   └────────────┬───────────┘    └──────────────┬───────────┘
                └───────────────┬───────────────┘
                     ┌──────────▼──────────┐
                     │ lighting             │  .Samples(…, shadowMap)
                     └──────────────────────┘
```

```csharp
var sun       = g.Domain("sun_shadow", 1024, 1024);     // a fixed-size square domain
var shadowMap = sun.Depth("sun_depth", Format.Depth32F);

g.Pass("shadow")
    .Reads(sunViewProj)
    .WritesDepth(shadowMap)
    .Draw(ctx => { /* draw casters with the "depthonly" technique */ });

g.Pass("gbuffer")
    .Reads(viewProj)
    .Writes(albedo, normal, position)
    .WritesDepth(depth)
    .Draw(ctx => { /* … */ });

g.Pass("lighting")
    .Samples(albedo, normal, position, shadowMap)
    .Writes(screen)
    .Draw(ctx => ctx.FullScreen("light_shadow", sunViewProjPush, albedo, normal, position, shadowMap));
```

The sun's view-projection rides the fullscreen push (`ctx.FullScreen(technique, push, inputs…)`) so the lighting shader can project each pixel into the same clip space the shadow pass drew with.

**Cascaded shadow maps** are the same shape scaled up: render N depth slices (cascades) fitted to slices of the camera frustum, then a `lighting_csm` pass selects a cascade per pixel by view depth and samples that slice. The cascade matrices and split distances ride the per-frame uniform channel.

---

## SSAO

Screen-space ambient occlusion: a G-buffer pass writes world position + normal; the `ssao` pass samples them and writes a single-channel occlusion term; a blur pass smooths the rotation noise; the lighting (or a view) pass then samples the blurred AO. Adding SSAO is just adding edges — `gbuffer → ssao → ssao.blur → lighting` — and the engine derives the ordering.

```
gbuffer { position, normal } ─► ssao ─► ssao.blur ─► (sampled by lighting)
                                 R16F      R16F
```

```csharp
var position = g.Screen.Color("position", Format.Rgba16F);
var normal   = g.Screen.Color("normal",   Format.Rgba16F);
var ao       = g.Screen.Color("ao",       Format.R16F);   // single-channel occlusion
var aoBlur   = g.Screen.Color("ao_blur",  Format.R16F);

g.Pass("ssao.calculate")
    .Samples(position, normal)
    .Writes(ao)
    .Draw(ctx => ctx.FullScreen("ssao", cameraViewProjPush, position, normal));

g.Pass("ssao.blur")
    .Samples(ao)
    .Writes(aoBlur)
    .Draw(ctx => ctx.FullScreen("ssao.blur", ao));

// the lighting pass then adds aoBlur to its .Samples and multiplies it into ambient
```

The AO target is `R16F`, not an 8-bit format. SSAO commonly runs in a half-resolution domain (`g.Domain("ssao", 0.5f)`) to save fill — allocate `ao`/`aoBlur` from that domain instead of `g.Screen` and the blur/sample chain follows.

---

## Bloom pyramid

Iterative downsample then additive upsample over a chain of progressively smaller mips. This is the canonical reusable graph fragment — it composes as a plain extension method on `GraphBuilder` and returns its output handle. The structure is **bright-pass → N downsamples → N−1 additive upsamples → composite**.

```
hdr ─► prefilter ─► mip0
                     │ down
                     ▼
                    mip1 ─ down ─► mip2 ─ down ─► … ─► mipN-1
                     ▲                                   │
                     │  up (.Blends, additive)           │
                     └──────────────◄────────────────────┘
        composite(source, mip0) ─► output
```

```csharp
public static ColorHandle Bloom(this GraphBuilder g, ColorHandle source, float threshold, int mips, float intensity)
{
    var domain = source.Domain;

    // The mip chain: each mip is half the size of the one above (scale 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, …).
    var chain = new ColorHandle[mips];
    for (var i = 0; i < mips; i++)
        chain[i] = domain.Color($"bloom_mip{i}", Format.Rgba16F, scale: 1f / (1 << (i + 1)));

    // Bright-pass + first halving into mip0 (threshold rides the fragment push).
    g.Pass("bloom.prefilter")
        .Samples(source)
        .Writes(chain[0])
        .Draw(ctx => ctx.FullScreen("bloom.prefilter", [threshold], source));

    // Downsample: each mip is the box-filtered half of the one above.
    for (var i = 1; i < mips; i++)
    {
        var (read, write) = (chain[i - 1], chain[i]);
        g.Pass($"bloom.down{i}")
            .Samples(read)
            .Writes(write)
            .Draw(ctx => ctx.FullScreen("bloom.down", read));
    }

    // Upsample from the smallest mip back up, additively accumulating into the larger mip the
    // downsample already wrote. .Blends (LoadOp.Load + additive) preserves + adds; the RAW edge
    // on each .Blends target forces the strict mipN → … → mip0 ordering.
    for (var i = mips - 2; i >= 0; i--)
    {
        var (smaller, larger) = (chain[i + 1], chain[i]);
        g.Pass($"bloom.up{i}")
            .Samples(smaller)
            .Blends(larger)
            .Draw(ctx => ctx.FullScreen("bloom.up", smaller));
    }

    // Composite the fully-accumulated mip0 back over the source into a fresh output — a plain
    // .Writes, so the bloom mips are dead afterwards and their memory can alias away.
    var output = domain.Color("lit_bloomed", Format.Rgba16F);
    g.Pass("bloom.composite")
        .Samples(source, chain[0])
        .Writes(output)
        .Draw(ctx => ctx.FullScreen("bloom.composite", [intensity], source, chain[0]));

    return output;
}
```

The `.Writes` vs `.Blends` distinction is load-bearing: the upsample passes `.Blends` the larger mip so the graph preserves the downsample's contents and accumulates onto them. A graph that only knew `.Writes` would lose the accumulation or miss the dependency.

### Instantiating a fragment more than once

Every name above is fixed — `bloom_mip0`, `bloom.prefilter`, `lit_bloomed` — and names are unique per graph, so calling `g.Bloom(…)` twice would collide. Wrap each call in a name scope instead of threading a prefix parameter through the fragment:

```csharp
ColorHandle left, right;
using (g.Scope("left"))  left  = g.Bloom(litLeft);
using (g.Scope("right")) right = g.Bloom(litRight);
```

The fragment is unchanged and unaware: its `bloom_mip0` becomes `left.bloom_mip0` and `right.bloom_mip0`, its passes become `left.bloom.prefilter` and so on, and the two chains derive as independent dependency chains. Scopes nest, and the qualified name is what the duplicate-name check and the graph hash see.

Two things are deliberately *not* scoped. **Techniques** are registered on the engine rather than declared on the graph, so `ctx.FullScreen("bloom.prefilter", …)` inside a scope still names the technique exactly as registered — only the pass sharing that name gets qualified. And the **backbuffer** keeps its identity whatever scope first touches it, since there is one swapchain image.

Pass names get a bonus: `DebugLabelScopes` derives the RenderDoc/PIX event tree from the same dots, so a scoped fragment's passes group under its scope in the capture with no extra work.

---

## GPU particles (compute → vertex)

A compute pass writes particle state into a storage buffer; a render pass reads that same buffer as a per-instance vertex stream and additively blends the sparks over the scene. Two edges — `.ReadWrites` then `.ReadsVertex` — and the engine derives the compute→vertex-input barrier between them (the one piece of sync unique to this effect).

```
particles (g.Buffer) ──.ReadWrites──► [compute: particle.update]
        │
        └──.ReadsVertex──► [draw: particle.render]  ──.Blends──► lit
```

```csharp
// A field, declared once beside the technique registration: one float4 per particle (xyz position + remaining life)
// as the per-instance stream at binding 0. "particle.render" names this same layout as its `Instance` stream, so the
// buffer's elements and the vertex stream that walks them cannot drift apart.
static readonly VertexLayout ParticleLayout = new(
    VertexInputRate.PerInstance, binding: 0,
    new VertexAttribute("POSITION", VertexFormat.Float4));

const int particleCount = 4096;
var particles = g.Buffer("particles", particleCount, ParticleLayout);   // sized count × the layout's 16-byte stride

g.Compute("particle.update")
    .ReadWrites(particles)
    .Dispatch(ctx => ctx.Dispatch(
        "particle.update",
        ((uint)(particleCount / 64), 1, 1),   // workgroup grid
        [ctx.Time],                            // up-to-16-float push block
        [],                                    // sampled inputs (none)
        [particles]));                         // read-write storage (the .ReadWrites resources)

g.Pass("particles")
    .Reads(viewProj)
    .Blends(lit)
    .ReadsVertex(particles)
    .Draw(ctx => ctx.Draw(new DrawCall
    {
        Technique = "particle.render",
        VertexCount = 6,                        // a billboard quad fabricated per particle from SV_VertexID
        Instances = DrawCall.Gpu(particles, particleCount),
    }));
```

`ctx.Dispatch` takes the workgroup grid as a `(uint X, uint Y, uint Z)` tuple, then three spans: the push block, the sampled inputs, and the read-write storage (matching the pass's `.Samples` / `.ReadWrites`). The render is a *procedural* draw — `Mesh` is null, `VertexCount` sets the per-instance vertex count, and `DrawCall.Gpu(buffer, count)` points the instance stream at the compute-filled buffer (CPU-sourced instances use `DrawCall.From(span)` instead).

Because the buffer was declared in terms of a layout rather than a byte count, both ways this can go wrong are caught on the CPU instead of reading past the end of the buffer on the GPU: `DrawCall.Gpu` rejects a `count` larger than the buffer holds, and the draw rejects a technique whose per-instance stream advances by a different stride than the buffer's elements.

---

## JFA outlines + GPU→CPU readback

A Jump Flood Algorithm builds a screen-space distance field to draw an outline, and a readback edge hands a picked object id back to the CPU. The cube writes its object id into an id target; that target is read back so the host knows which object the cursor is over; a seed pass marks the hovered object's pixels and a jump-flood ping-pong (steps 4→2→1) propagates the nearest seed; a resolve pass turns nearest-seed distance into an emissive ring composited over the lit scene. Runs in a fixed `320×180` domain so the flood has concrete pixel dimensions and the cursor maps cleanly.

```
scene ─► lit
  └─► id (R16F) ──► g.Readback(id) ─ ─ ─► host: engine.Read(id) at the cursor → hoveredId
                                                   │ (next frame, via a constants channel)
                                                   ▼
   seed ─► [jfa step4] ─► [jfa step2] ─► [jfa step1] ─► resolve(flood, lit) ─► outlined
            (Rg16F ping-pong: read/write handles swapped each iteration)
```

```csharp
var world = g.Domain("world", 320, 180);
var lit   = world.Color("lit",       Format.Rgba16F);
var ids   = world.Color("object_id", Format.R16F);     // id target (R16F here; R32Uint for large id ranges)
var seedA = world.Color("outline_a", Format.Rg16F);    // JFA stores nearest-seed coords
var seedB = world.Color("outline_b", Format.Rg16F);

// Write the cube's object id (the id rides the per-draw uniform block), then read it back.
g.Pass("id")
    .Reads(viewProj)
    .Writes(ids)
    .Draw(ctx => { /* draw cube with the "id" technique; SetUniforms the id */ });
g.Readback(ids);

g.Pass("outline.seed")
    .Samples(ids)
    .Reads(hoverParams)        // the host writes the hovered id into this constants channel
    .Writes(seedA)
    .Draw(ctx => ctx.FullScreen("outline.seed", ids));

// Ping-pong via handle swap (the handle-swap pillar) — two physical targets, swapped each step.
var (read, write) = (seedA, seedB);
for (var step = 4; step >= 1; step >>= 1)
{
    var src = read;            // capture per-iteration so the closure follows this step's handle
    float jump = step;
    g.Pass($"outline.jfa{step}")
        .Samples(src)
        .Writes(write)
        .Draw(ctx => ctx.FullScreen("outline.jfa", [jump, world.Width, world.Height], src));
    (read, write) = (write, read);   // swap; the next pass reads what this one wrote
}

var flood = read;              // the final flood after the swaps
g.Pass("outline.resolve")
    .Samples(flood, lit)
    .Writes(outlined)
    .Draw(ctx => ctx.FullScreen("outline.resolve", flood, lit));
```

**Reading the pick result.** There is no engine picking state and no `FrameInputs` hover field. The host queries the readback target directly with `IEngine.Read(handle)`, which returns the target's texels tightly packed in its declared format, a frame or two old:

```csharp
// host side, after Render: decode the id under the cursor (the id target is R16F → Half)
var (pw, ph) = idTarget.Resolve();                         // the target's own resolution
var pixels   = MemoryMarshal.Cast<byte, Half>(engine.Read(idTarget));
var i        = cursorY * pw + cursorX;
uint hoverId = i < pixels.Length ? (uint)MathF.Round((float)pixels[i]) : 0u;
// feed it back for next frame's seed pass:
engine.Write(hoverParams, new OutlineParams(hoverId));
```

The latency is real (the copy is from a frame the GPU has finished, so it never races in-flight work) — the picked id arrives one to two frames later and is fed into the *next* frame's seed pass through an ordinary constants channel.

---

## Auto-exposure + tonemap

Two-stage HDR grading: a compute pass meters the lit scene's average luminance into a tiny **persistent** 1×1 target that carries across frames (so the adaptation is temporal), then a tone-map pass scales by that exposure and rolls off the highlights to the display. This is the GPU→persistent→GPU loop plus the compute→fragment hand-off the engine derives.

```
lit ──.Samples──► [compute: exposure] ──.ReadWrites──► exposure (1×1 Persistent, R16F)
                                                              │ carried frame to frame
 lit ─┬──.Samples──────────────────────────────────.Samples─┘
      └──► [tonemap] ──► graded
```

```csharp
var lit      = g.Screen.Color("lit", Format.Rgba16F);
var meter    = g.Domain("meter", 1, 1);                       // a fixed 1×1 domain
var exposure = meter.Persistent("exposure", Format.R16F);     // cross-frame, NOT a g.Buffer
var graded   = g.Screen.Color("graded", Format.Rgba16F);

// Meter the lit scene's luminance into the 1×1 persistent exposure (the adaptation rate rides the push).
g.Compute("exposure")
    .Samples(lit)
    .ReadWrites(exposure)
    .Dispatch(ctx => ctx.Dispatch("exposure", (1, 1, 1), [8f * ctx.DeltaTime], [lit], [exposure]));

// Scale by exposure + roll off highlights (SDR), or preserve the extended range for HDR output.
g.Pass("tonemap")
    .Samples(lit, exposure)
    .Writes(graded)
    .Draw(ctx => ctx.FullScreen("tonemap", [ctx.HdrOutput ? 1f : 0f], lit, exposure));
```

The exposure history is a `domain.Persistent(...)` target, not a storage buffer — a persistent target keeps its contents across frames so this frame's metering reads last frame's value and eases toward the new one. The dispatch is a single 1×1×1 group reducing the whole image; the adaptation rate (here `8 · ΔtimeDelta`) rides the push block.

---

## Forward alpha-blend transparency

A forward pass that blends translucent geometry over the deferred opaque result. It `.Blends` the lit colour (load + alpha-over) and `.ReadsDepth` the opaque depth (depth-tested but read-only), so the opaque scene occludes the transparent geometry without the transparent pass clearing or writing depth.

```
(opaque lit + depth)
        │  .Blends(lit)  + .ReadsDepth(depth)
        ▼
   transparent ─► lit (blended in place)
```

```csharp
engine.DefineTechnique("transparent",
    new TechniqueDescriptor("transparent", HasVertexInput: true, Blend: BlendMode.AlphaOver));

g.Pass("transparent")
    .Reads(viewProj)
    .Blends(lit)
    .ReadsDepth(depth)
    .Draw(ctx => ctx.Draw(DrawCall.Create(transparentMesh, "transparent")));
```

`.Blends` + `.ReadsDepth` = depth-tested, depth-read-only, colour-blended. No `.WritesDepth` means no depth clear — the opaque depth buffer stays intact and keeps occluding. The same shape with `Blend: BlendMode.Additive` (and a depth test) is how emissive volumes, a glowing summoning ring, or additive 2D light volumes layer onto a lit scene.

---

## Low-resolution world + upscale

A fixed-pixel-art domain renders at a constant size regardless of window dimensions; a final fullscreen pass samples that low-res target up to the backbuffer. The upscale *is* the pixelation — nearest-neighbour sampling keeps the pixels crisp.

```
       g.Domain("world", 320, 180)            g.Backbuffer (native)
   ┌──────────────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────┐
   │  scene → … → world (Rgba16F)  │ ─────► │  upscale (blit)      │
   └──────────────────────────────┘ sample └──────────────────────┘
```

```csharp
var world  = g.Domain("world", 320, 180);              // fixed size, not window-relative
var lit    = world.Color("lit", Format.Rgba16F);
var screen = g.Backbuffer;

g.Pass("scene")
    .Writes(lit)
    .WritesDepth(world.Depth("depth", Format.Depth32F))
    .Draw(ctx => { /* render the world at 320×180 */ });

g.Pass("upscale")
    .Samples(lit)
    .Writes(screen)
    .Draw(ctx => ctx.FullScreen("blit", lit));

g.Present(screen);
```

`ctx.FullScreen` with a single input is the blit/upscale path — a fullscreen *sample* of the source at the output resolution, not a copy. The `blit` shader ships in Loom's shared shader library; you still register it as a technique (`engine.DefineTechnique("blit", new TechniqueDescriptor("blit"))`) — define it without `LinearFilter` for the nearest-neighbour, pixel-art-clean look. A full pixel-art scene typically inserts a `g.Bloom(lit, …)` between the world and the upscale so the lights and sparks glow before they're enlarged.

---

# Audio

How to make sound in a Loom app: clips played on voices, mixed through buses, and **sources**, sound the game writes
itself sample by sample (software synthesizers, procedural engine notes, generated music). Then what runs on which
thread, and what each platform does underneath.

[`Loom.Audio`](../Loom.Audio) holds the mixer and depends only on the BCL, as `Loom.Input` does. Each host opens its
platform's output device behind one seam, `IAudioDevice`:

| Host | Device | Where the mix runs | Latency the mix adds |
|---|---|---|---|
| Desktop (`Loom.Hosting.Desktop`) | SDL 3, the system's default output | SDL's audio thread | one device buffer: 480 frames (10 ms) on Windows, the floor of shared-mode WASAPI |
| Android (`Loom.Hosting.Android`) | AAudio, low-latency, exclusive where the device allows | AAudio's callback thread | two bursts: 192 frames (4 ms) on a Galaxy S23 Ultra's exclusive MMAP path |
| Browser (`Loom.Hosting.Web`) | an AudioWorklet | the frame thread, 50 ms ahead of the speaker | the 50 ms lead, by design (see [The browser](#the-browser)) |

`samples/HelloAudio` is a whole app built on all of it: an eight-voice synthesizer played from the keyboard, an
arpeggiator timed on the audio clock, and a clip fired from the game. It builds as a desktop exe, an Android APK and a
browser app from the same source.

Sound built on top of the mixer (rendering offline to measure it or save it as a WAV file) is in
[`Loom.Audio.Synth`](../Loom.Audio.Synth), and [the synthesis guide](synth.md) covers it.

---

## 1. Turning it on

Set `AppOptions.Audio` in `Configure`, then play through `LoomApplication.Audio`:

```csharp
sealed class MyGame : LoomApplication
{
	private AudioBus _sfx;
	private AudioClip _hit = null!;

	protected override void Configure(AppOptions options) =>
		options.Audio = new AudioOptions(); // the device's own rate and its smallest buffer

	protected override void LoadContent()
	{
		_sfx = Audio.CreateBus("sfx");
		_hit = Audio.LoadWav(ReadContent("sounds/hit.wav"));
	}

	protected override void Update(FrameTime time)
	{
		if (Input.Pressed(Key.Space))
			Audio.Play(_hit, _sfx, volume: 0.8f, pitch: 1.1f, pan: -0.3f);
	}
}
```

`LoomApplication` runs the engine through the app's lifecycle, so an app never opens, pumps or closes it:

| When | What happens |
|---|---|
| Before `LoadContent` | The host opens its output device and the app's `AudioEngine` starts it. The log names the backend, the output, the rate and the buffer granted. |
| Every tick, after `Update` and `BeforeRender` | `Audio.Update()`: frees the voices that ended and throws what a source threw on the audio thread. |
| `OnSuspending` / `OnResumed` | The device pauses after `OnSuspending` and resumes before `OnResumed`. Voices hold where they are. |
| The window or tab loses or regains focus | `Audio.SetFocused`, before `OnFocusChanged`: the output fades to `AudioOptions.UnfocusedVolume` and back (see below). |
| After `UnloadContent` | The engine closes the device. |

With `AppOptions.Audio` left null, audio is off and reading `Audio` throws.

### `AudioOptions`

Every value is a request the platform meets as closely as it can. `Audio.Device` says what was granted.

| Option | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `SampleRate` | 0 (the device's own) | The mixing rate. Any rate but the device's own makes the platform resample, which adds latency. |
| `BufferFrames` | 0 (the smallest the backend offers) | The device buffer, which is the latency the mixer adds. Raise it only if the output crackles on a slow device. In the browser it is the lead ahead of the speaker. |
| `MaxVoices` | 64 | Voices playing at once, clips and sources together. A play past it is dropped (see [Voices](#3-voices)). |
| `MaxBuses` | 16 | Buses, the master bus included. |
| `MaxDucks` | 8 | Ducks (see [Ducking](#ducking)). |
| `MaxEffectsPerBus` | 8 | Effects on one bus (see [Effects and sends](#effects-and-sends)). |
| `MaxSends` | 16 | Sends between buses. |
| `SpeedOfSound` | 343 | The speed of sound in the game's units a second, for the Doppler shift of 3D voices: 343 for metres, 1125 for feet. |
| `UnfocusedVolume` | 1 (no change) | The output's volume while the app is out of focus: another window in front, the browser tab hidden, the app behind another on Android. The whole mix fades to it over a quarter second and back on return. 0 silences an app in the background. It is a gain of its own after the master bus, so the game's volumes, the master's included, are left alone, and it multiplies with them. `Audio.SetUnfocusedVolume` changes it while the app runs, for a setting the player chooses. |
| `CommandCapacity` | 4096 | Commands (plays, stops, volume changes) waiting for the audio thread at once. Past it the engine throws rather than drop one. |
| `Work` | `Thread` | Where the work off the audio thread runs (decoding streams, rendering [ahead sources](#ahead-of-the-speaker-aheadsource)): `AudioWork.Thread`, a worker thread of the engine's, or `AudioWork.Update`, in `Audio.Update()` on the frame thread, which is deterministic (tests and offline renders; `OfflineSession` takes it by default). In the browser `Thread` is taken as `Update` unless `BrowserThread`. |
| `BrowserThread` | false | In the browser, give the work its own thread as on the desktop, rather than the frame thread. A thread made while a browser app runs can hang its frames, so set `StartWorker` with it. |
| `StartWorker` | false | Make the worker as the engine is made, rather than when the first stream or ahead source needs it. |

### No output

When a host can't open an output (no device, or SDL3 missing on the desktop), it hands the engine a `NullAudioDevice`
and logs a warning saying why. A `NullAudioDevice` renders in real time and drops what it renders, so voices still
advance and end, and a game that waits on a sound finishing behaves as it would with a speaker. A machine with no
speaker is not a bug in the app, so this is not an error.

---

## 2. Clips

A clip is sound decoded into memory, ready to play any number of times at once: a footstep, a hit, a loop.

```csharp
var hit = Audio.LoadWav(ReadContent("sounds/hit.wav"));            // a WAV file's bytes
var step = Audio.LoadOgg(ReadContent("sounds/step.ogg"));          // an Ogg Vorbis file's bytes
var bell = Audio.LoadFlac(ReadContent("sounds/bell.flac"));        // a FLAC file's bytes
var beep = Audio.CreateClip(samples, channels: 1, sampleRate: 44_100); // samples the app made, -1..1
```

- `LoadWav` reads RIFF/WAVE files: PCM at 8, 16, 24 or 32 bits, and IEEE float at 32 or 64, mono or stereo
  (`WAVE_FORMAT_EXTENSIBLE` included). Any other format throws `NotSupportedException`, and bytes that aren't a WAV
  file throw `InvalidDataException`.
- `LoadOgg` decodes an Ogg Vorbis file whole, mono or stereo. A file with more channels throws
  `NotSupportedException`, and bytes that aren't Ogg Vorbis, or are damaged, throw `InvalidDataException`. For music,
  stream instead (below): a clip holds every decoded sample, ten times the file's size or more.
- `LoadFlac` decodes a FLAC file whole, mono or stereo, at any bit depth from 4 to 32. FLAC is lossless, at about half
  the size of the same audio as WAV: for sounds whose detail Vorbis would smear. The same exceptions apply.
- All of them convert the clip to the engine's rate as it loads, so playing it never resamples (a pitch other than 1 aside).
  The conversion is a 4-point Hermite curve, which doesn't filter on the way down: a 96 kHz clip loaded at 48 kHz can
  alias faintly. Supply clips at the engine's rate where that matters.
- **Any thread may make a clip.** Decode on a loading thread (`ReadContentAsync`) and play on the frame thread.
- Code that keeps samples itself (a synthesizer's sample player, a tool) decodes without an engine:
  `AudioDecoder.DecodeWav`, `DecodeOgg`, `DecodeFlac`, or `Decode` (any of them, by the file's first four bytes) give an
  `AudioData` at the file's own rate, with the same exceptions.
- A clip belongs to the engine whose rate it was made at. Playing it on an engine at another rate throws.

### Streams

Music is streamed: decoded as it plays, from an Ogg Vorbis or FLAC file held compressed. `OpenStream` tells which from
the file's first bytes. An `AudioStream` is a source, so it plays, fades, pans and stops like one.

```csharp
_theme = Audio.OpenStream(ReadContent("music/theme.ogg"), loop: true);
Audio.Play(_theme, music);
// ... later
Audio.Stop(_theme, fadeSeconds: 2f);
_theme.Dispose(); // once it has faded, or when the game is done with it
```

- **Each play starts from the beginning.** A looping stream joins its end to its start without a gap, to the sample:
  the file's length is exactly what was encoded (an Ogg file's last page's granule position says so; a FLAC file's
  frames hold exactly its samples).
- **Decoding never happens on the audio thread.** The engine's worker thread decodes about half a second ahead into a
  lock-free ring, waking every 10 ms, and the audio thread reads the ring. With `AudioWork.Update` (and in the browser,
  where the mix runs on the frame thread, by default), `Audio.Update()` decodes ahead instead. A play decodes the first 100 ms on the calling
  thread, so the stream has sound from its first block.
- **A file at another rate is converted as it plays,** by the same curve clips are converted with. A 44.1 kHz file
  plays at the right pitch and speed on a 48 kHz device.
- `OpenStream(byte[])` takes the file's bytes, as `ReadContent` gives them. `OpenStream(Stream)` reads a file stream as
  it plays, off the audio thread; a stream that can't seek (an Android asset's) is read into memory first, so that it
  can loop and play again. The `AudioStream` owns the stream and closes it.
- Opening a file checks its headers, so a file that is neither Ogg Vorbis nor FLAC throws there. Damage further in
  throws `InvalidOperationException` (the decoder's exception inside it) from the next `Audio.Update()`, and the stream
  stops.
- Decoding costs little: Vorbis and FLAC both decode at over 250 times real time for 44.1 kHz stereo on a Snapdragon X
  core, so a stream takes well under 1% of a core.
- `Dispose` stops a playing stream at once and closes its file. Disposing the engine closes every stream.

The decoder is Loom's own, written from the Vorbis I specification: no native library, the same code on every
platform, and it allocates nothing once a stream is open. It decodes what every encoder since libvorbis 1.0 writes,
matching libvorbis to its last bit of 16-bit output (`VorbisDecoderTests`); floor type 0, which nothing has written
since 2002, throws `NotSupportedException`.

The FLAC decoder is Loom's own too, written from RFC 9639, and also allocates nothing once open. It is bit-exact: its
tests check every decoded sample against the MD5 each file carries (`FlacDecoderTests`), and it decodes all of the
IETF working group's conformance files with samples to check, 32-bit and 768 kHz included. It checks every frame's
checksums, so a damaged file throws rather than playing noise. It skips ID3 tags before and after the audio. It
refuses (`NotSupportedException`) a file that changes its rate or channel count partway, and doesn't read FLAC inside
Ogg or a file that starts without its `fLaC` header.

---

## 3. Voices

Every play takes a voice from a fixed pool and returns a `VoiceHandle`:

```csharp
var engineLoop = Audio.Play(_engineClip, _sfx, loop: true);
Audio.SetPitch(engineLoop, 0.8f + rpm / 8000f);
Audio.SetVolume(engineLoop, 0.5f, fadeSeconds: 0.2f);
Audio.SetPan(engineLoop, -0.4f);
Audio.Stop(engineLoop, fadeSeconds: 0.5f);
```

| Member | What it does |
|---|---|
| `Play(clip, bus, volume, pitch, pan, loop)` | Plays a clip. `pitch` 2 is an octave up and twice as fast. `pan` runs -1 (left) to 1 (right). A looping clip plays until stopped. |
| `Play(source, bus, volume, pan)` | Plays a source (see [Sources](#5-sources)) until it finishes or is stopped. |
| `SetVolume(voice, volume, fadeSeconds)` | Moves a voice's volume, a linear gain. |
| `SetPitch(voice, pitch)` | A clip voice's pitch. A source voice ignores it. |
| `SetPan(voice, pan)` | Moves the pan across the next block. |
| `Stop(voice, fadeSeconds)` / `Stop(source, fadeSeconds)` | Fades the voice out, then ends it. |
| `IsPlaying(voice)` | Whether the voice still plays, as the frame thread last heard (at most a frame old). |

Things to know:

- **Nothing clicks.** Every change of volume, pan or bus volume ramps across at least one block (256 frames at most,
  about 5 ms at 48 kHz). A stop with no fade still ramps to silence over one block.
- **A handle goes stale when its voice ends,** and the engine ignores a stale handle rather than reach the voice that
  took its slot. A game can keep handles without tracking when each sound finishes.
- **When every voice is busy, a play is dropped.** It returns `VoiceHandle.None` and adds one to
  `Stats.DroppedVoices`. Raise `AudioOptions.MaxVoices` if that happens in normal play.
- A mono clip pans at equal power (-3 dB in each side at the centre). A stereo clip or a source pans as a balance: it
  keeps its own image and turns down the side it pans away from.

### Voices in 3D

A voice played with `PlayAt` has a position instead of a pan. Each block, the engine places it for the listener: panned
by which side of the listener it is on, quieter with distance, and pitch-shifted by motion (Doppler).

```csharp
// Each frame, from the game's camera (the engine takes positions, never a camera)
Audio.SetListener(camera.Position, camera.Forward, camera.Up, cameraVelocity);

var engineHum = Audio.PlayAt(_humClip, car.Position, _sfx, loop: true,
	spatial: new AudioSpatial { MinDistance = 2f, MaxDistance = 80f });
Audio.SetPosition(engineHum, car.Position, car.Velocity);  // each frame it moves
Audio.PlayAt(_footstep, foot.Position, _sfx);                // a one-shot where it happened
```

| Member | What it does |
|---|---|
| `SetListener(position, forward, up, velocity)` | Where the game hears from. Call it each frame the listener moves. Until it is set, the listener is at the origin facing -Z, with +Y up. |
| `PlayAt(clip, position, bus, volume, pitch, loop, spatial)` | Plays a clip as a 3D voice. |
| `PlayAt(source, position, bus, volume, spatial)` | Plays a source (a stream included) as a 3D voice. |
| `SetPosition(voice, position, velocity)` | Moves a 3D voice, heard from the next block. |

`AudioSpatial` sets how a voice falls off and shifts. Its distances are in the game's units, as its positions are:

| Property | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `MinDistance` | 1 | Within this, full volume. |
| `MaxDistance` | 100 | Beyond this, no quieter. |
| `Rolloff` | `Inverse` | The curve between the two: `Inverse` (halves at twice the minimum distance; how sound falls off in the open), `Linear` (a straight fade to silence at the maximum distance), or `Exponential`. They are OpenAL's clamped models. |
| `RolloffFactor` | 1 | How steep the curve is: 0 doesn't fall off, 2 is twice as steep. |
| `DopplerFactor` | 1 | How much motion shifts the pitch: 0 never, 1 as sound really does, more to exaggerate it. |

- **Right-handed,** as `Matrix4x4.CreateLookAt` is: the listener's right is forward × up.
- **Stereo panning only:** a voice's pan is how far to the listener's right it is. Two speakers can't tell front from
  back, so a voice behind the listener sounds where its mirror in front would. There is no HRTF.
- **A 3D voice is one point.** A stereo clip or source is heard with its two channels mixed, then panned at equal power.
- **Doppler comes from the velocities the game gives,** the voice's and the listener's, not from how far they moved
  between frames, which would jitter with the frame rate. A voice given no velocity isn't shifted. The shift is held
  within two octaves either way. A source has no pitch, so it isn't shifted.
- **Volume and pitch still apply:** `SetVolume` scales the voice under its distance gain, and `SetPitch` multiplies with
  the Doppler shift. `SetPan` on a 3D voice throws, as does `SetPosition` on a voice played with `Play`.
- Everything moves smoothly: the distance gain and the pan ramp across each block, and a 3D voice is placed before its
  first block, so it never starts at the centre at full volume.

---

## 4. Buses

Buses group voices so they can be set as one: music, sound effects, UI. They form a tree under `Audio.Master`, each
mixed into its parent.

```csharp
var music = Audio.CreateBus("music");
var sfx = Audio.CreateBus("sfx");
var footsteps = Audio.CreateBus("footsteps", parent: sfx);

Audio.SetBusVolume(music, 0.3f, fadeSeconds: 1f); // everything in music follows it
```

- Make buses at load. There are at most `AudioOptions.MaxBuses`, and none is ever removed.
- The engine names only the master bus. Every other bus, and its name, is the app's.
- The mix order follows from the tree (children before parents), so an app never orders buses itself.
- The master bus is clipped to -1..1 on its way to the device. `Stats.Peak` reports the loudest sample before that
  clip, so a peak above 1 means the mix is too loud.

### Ducking

A duck turns one bus down while another has sound on it: music under dialogue, ambience under a cutscene.

```csharp
var dialogue = Audio.CreateBus("dialogue");
var music = Audio.CreateBus("music");
var duck = Audio.AddDuck(trigger: dialogue, target: music, depthDb: -9f, attackSeconds: 0.05f, releaseSeconds: 0.4f);

Audio.SetDuckEnabled(duck, false); // music back up, however loud the dialogue
```

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `depthDb` | (required) | How far down the target goes, in decibels, below zero: -6 halves it, -12 is a quarter. |
| `attackSeconds` | 0.05 | How long the target takes to go all the way down. |
| `releaseSeconds` | 0.4 | How long it takes to come all the way back. |
| `thresholdDb` | -40 | The trigger's level, in decibels of full scale, above which it counts as sounding. |
| `holdSeconds` | 0.15 | How long the target stays down after the trigger falls quiet, so it doesn't pump up between words. |

- **A duck follows the trigger's level, not its voices.** The target comes back up in a pause in the dialogue, and a
  source playing silence ducks nothing. The level is the trigger bus's peak after its own volume, so turning the
  dialogue bus down to nothing stops it ducking.
- **The duck acts a block after it hears.** Each block's ducks are worked out from the last block's levels, so the order
  buses were made in doesn't matter. The block of delay (a few milliseconds) sits inside any attack.
- A bus several ducks turn down takes all their depths: two -6 dB ducks sounding at once make -12 dB.
- **A duck can't involve a bus that contains the other.** Ducking a bus the trigger is mixed into (the master, say) would
  turn the trigger down too, and ducking a bus mixed into the trigger would lower the trigger's level and let the duck
  go, so it would pump. Both throw.
- Make ducks at load, like buses. There are at most `AudioOptions.MaxDucks`, and none is removed: `SetDuckEnabled`
  turns one off, and its target comes back up at its release rate.

### Effects and sends

An effect changes the sound passing through a bus: a reverb, a limiter, a distortion. Subclass `AudioEffect`, write
`Process`, and add it to a bus. A send mixes a share of one bus into another as well as into its parent, which is how
several buses share one reverb.

```csharp
var sfx = Audio.CreateBus("sfx");
var space = Audio.CreateBus("space");          // the room several buses send to
Audio.AddEffect(space, new Reverb());          // Loom.Audio.Synth.Effects; Wet 1, Dry 0 suit a bus fed by sends
var toSpace = Audio.AddSend(sfx, space, 0.1f);
Audio.AddEffect(Audio.Master, new Limiter());

Audio.SetSendLevel(toSpace, 0.4f, fadeSeconds: 0.2f); // more of the sound off the walls
```

- **The order within a bus is its effects, then its volume, then its ducks.** Effects run on everything mixed into
  the bus, before its volume, so a reverb's tail is turned down by the bus's volume with everything else. They run in
  the order added. On the master bus they run before the focus volume and the final clip.
- **Buses and sends are made in any order.** The engine works out the order to mix them in from what feeds what: a bus
  is finished before the bus it is mixed into and before the buses it sends to, so each receives the whole of what is
  sent to it. A send that would make a loop (a bus sending to one mixed into it, or round through other sends), a send
  to itself or to a bus it is already mixed into, and a send from the master throw. The sound sent is the bus's after
  its effects, volume and ducks.
- `Process` runs on the audio thread under the rules for a source's `Render` ([The rules for `Render`](#the-rules-for-render)):
  size buffers in `OnPrepare`, which `AddEffect` calls on the game thread. Its controls are `AudioParameter` and
  `SmoothedParameter` members of its own.
- An effect instance belongs to one bus: adding it to a second throws. `AudioEffect.Prepare`, `Run` and `Process` are
  public so a synthesizer can run effects on groups of its own voices.
- **An effect costs nothing while nothing plays through it.** The mixer calls `Run`, which calls `Process` unless
  silence (120 dB under full scale) has gone in and come out for the effect's `MemorySeconds`: then the effect rests,
  the block is left alone, and it starts again with the first sound. A reverb's tail and a delay's echoes are heard out
  first. `MemorySeconds` is 1 by default; override it in an effect with a longer delay (`Delay` gives its longest time),
  or return infinity from one that makes sound of its own, which never rests. `IsResting` says whether it is. A song
  whose distorted guitar plays in one section pays for the distortion only there: two test songs rendered twice as
  fast, the same sample for sample.
- An effect that throws is skipped from then on, the sound passing unchanged, and the exception is thrown from the next
  `Audio.Update`, as a source's is.
- Add effects and sends at load. A bus holds at most `AudioOptions.MaxEffectsPerBus`, the engine at most
  `AudioOptions.MaxSends`, and none is removed: `Bypass` turns an effect off, and a level of 0 silences a send.
- `Loom.Audio.Synth`'s `Effects` namespace has a reverb, delay, chorus, compressor, limiter, EQ and distortion
  (`docs/synth.md`, "Effects").

---

## 5. Sources

A source is sound the game writes itself. Subclass `AudioSource`, write `Render`, and play it like a clip:

```csharp
sealed class Sine : AudioSource
{
	public AudioParameter Frequency { get; } = new(440f);
	private float _phase, _rate;

	// The frame thread, as the source starts playing: size buffers and work out coefficients here
	protected override void OnStart(int sampleRate) => _rate = sampleRate;

	// The audio thread, once a block
	protected override bool Render(Span<float> left, Span<float> right, in AudioRenderInfo info)
	{
		var frequency = Frequency.Ramp(info.Frames); // glides across the block: no click when it changes
		for (var i = 0; i < info.Frames; i++)
		{
			left[i] = right[i] = 0.2f * MathF.Sin(2 * MathF.PI * _phase);
			_phase = (_phase + frequency.Next() / _rate) % 1f;
		}
		return true; // false ends the voice
	}
}

var sine = new Sine();
Audio.Play(sine, music);
sine.Frequency.Value = 660f; // from the game, any time
```

### The rules for `Render`

`Render` runs on the audio thread, once a block of up to 256 frames, against a deadline: a block late is heard as a
click or a dropout.

- **Don't allocate.** A garbage collection pauses every managed thread, the audio thread included, so an allocation in
  `Render` is the one thing in the source's control that can stall the mix. Allocate in the constructor or `OnStart`.
- **Don't lock, block or wait,** and don't call anything that might (I/O, logging, `Console`).
- The spans arrive zeroed and hold `info.Frames` samples each. Write both, even for a mono sound.
- Return false once the source has finished. Its voice ends and the source can be played again.
- **An exception thrown in `Render` stops the voice** and is thrown again on the frame thread from the next
  `Audio.Update()`, wrapped in an `InvalidOperationException`. The audio thread itself carries on.

`AudioRenderInfo` carries the block's `Frames`, the engine's `SampleRate`, and `FrameTime`: how many frames the engine
had rendered before this block. `FrameTime` is the audio clock, so a sequencer or arpeggiator counts beats on it and
stays sample-accurate however the frame rate wanders. It runs only while the device does.

### One voice at a time

A source keeps its own state, so it plays on one voice at a time, and playing it while it plays throws. It counts as
playing from its `Play` until the engine hears its voice end, which after `Stop` is once the audio thread has rendered
the fade. So `Stop(source)` followed at once by `Play(source)` throws. Play it again once `source.IsPlaying` is false,
or make another instance. Each `Play` of a source hears the voices that have ended, so a source that finished or faded
out since the last frame can be played again straight away.

### Steering a source from the game

The game and the audio thread share no lock, so a source takes its controls through these lock-free types:

| Type | For | Game thread | Audio thread |
|---|---|---|---|
| `AudioParameter` | A continuous value where only the latest matters, reached within the block: a cutoff, a level set from a menu. | Set `Value` whenever it likes. | `Ramp(info.Frames)` once a block, then `Next()` once a sample: a straight line from where it was to `Value`. `Snap()` jumps straight there, for a control where a step is what's wanted (a waveform choice). |
| `SmoothedParameter` | A continuous value the game moves often and in steps, eased with a time constant (`seconds`, after which it has gone 63% of the way): a motor's revs, a wind's strength, set every physics step. An `AudioParameter` would follow it as a staircase of short ramps. | Set `Value` whenever it likes. | `Prepare(rate)` in `OnStart`; `Begin()` once a block, then `Next()` once a sample, or `Skip(frames)` for a value read once a block. `Snap()` jumps straight there. |
| `AudioEventQueue<T>` | Discrete events that must all arrive, in order: note on, note off, a trigger. `T` is a small struct. | `TryPost(event)` (false when full), or `Post`, which throws when full. | `TryTake(out event)` at the start of `Render`, until it returns false. |

An `AudioEventQueue<T>` has a fixed capacity (rounded up to a power of two) and is strictly one thread posting and one
taking. Two threads posting to the same queue corrupt it.

```csharp
readonly record struct NoteEvent(int Note, float Velocity, bool On);

sealed class Synth : AudioSource
{
	public AudioEventQueue<NoteEvent> Notes { get; } = new(256);

	protected override bool Render(Span<float> left, Span<float> right, in AudioRenderInfo info)
	{
		while (Notes.TryTake(out var note))
		{
			if (note.On)
				NoteOn(note.Note, note.Velocity);
			else
				NoteOff(note.Note);
		}
		// ... render the voices
		return true;
	}
}

synth.Notes.TryPost(new NoteEvent(60, 0.9f, On: true)); // from Update
```

### Ahead of the speaker: `AheadSource`

A source that costs a lot to render, and can answer its controls a little late, can be rendered ahead of the speaker,
off the audio thread:

```csharp
_music = new AheadSource(Audio, songSource, leadSeconds: 0.1);
Audio.Play(_music, musicBus);
```

- **The engine's worker renders the inner source** in blocks of 256 frames into a lock-free ring, keeping the lead
  waiting and waking every 2 ms while there are ahead sources (with `AudioWork.Update`, `Audio.Update()` does it). The
  audio thread only copies from the ring, so its cost there is a copy, whatever the inner source costs.
- **The lead is latency.** A change to the inner source's controls is heard up to the lead later. Music can take that
  (the music player's `aheadSeconds`, [synth.md](synth.md)); a sound effect, a sound that follows the player's hands or a click
  of the UI should play directly.
- **A play doesn't stall the frame.** With a worker, the worker renders the first lead and the source is silent until
  it is waiting (a few milliseconds), which isn't counted as an underrun; rendering it on the frame thread cost a song of
  nine tracks 9 ms there. With `AudioWork.Update` (tests, offline renders) the play renders the lead at once, so it
  sounds from its first block and a render is the same however it is run.
- **If the work falls behind,** the block plays silence where nothing waits, counted in `Underruns`, and the source
  carries on from where it stopped, none of it lost. `FramesHeard` and `FramesRendered` say how far each side has got.
- **The inner source must not play on its own** while wrapped (a play of it throws), and its controls keep one reader:
  the thread rendering it ahead, in place of the audio thread. What the inner source throws is thrown again from
  `Audio.Update()`, as a stream's fault is. `Dispose` stops it and takes it out of the worker's list.

`AheadSourceTests` holds it to that: frames in order with none lost, the lead kept, an underrun counted and recovered
from, the end and a fault passed on, nothing allocated once it plays, and a real-time device kept up with by the worker.

---

## 6. Threads

Three threads share an `AudioEngine`:

- **The frame thread** (the thread that made the engine, the app's in a `LoomApplication`) calls every method. A call
  from any other thread throws, except making clips (`CreateClip`, `LoadWav`), which touches no shared state.
- **The audio thread** (the device's) mixes. It never waits on the game.
- **The worker** (`Loom audio worker`), when streams or ahead sources need it (or at once, with `StartWorker`):
  decodes streams ahead and renders ahead sources ahead. It never touches the mix; with `AudioWork.Update` there is
  none, and `Update` does its work.

| Thread | Runs | Wakes |
|---|---|---|
| Frame | every engine call; `Update` | each frame |
| Audio | the mix: sources' `Render`, effects, buses | each device buffer (10 ms on Windows) |
| Worker | streams' decoding, ahead sources' rendering | every 2 ms with ahead sources, 10 ms without |

Each call on the frame thread copies a command into a lock-free queue, and the audio thread takes the queued commands at
the start of its next block. So a play is heard within one device buffer of the call, and the order of calls is the
order they take effect. The audio thread answers through a second queue (the voices that ended, which `Update` frees)
and through `Stats`.

Once running, neither side allocates: not a play, a stop, a volume change, or a block of the mix.
`AudioEngineTests.The_mix_allocates_nothing_once_running` holds the engine to that. The game's own allocations still
matter: a garbage collection the game sets off pauses the audio thread too. A game that keeps its steady frame free of
allocations, as Loom's render loop is, keeps its audio safe as well.

### Watching the mix

`Audio.Stats` reports how the mix is doing, for a debug display or a test:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `FramesRendered`, `Callbacks`, `LastCallbackFrames` | The mix's clock, how many times the device has asked for samples, and the buffer it is really running at. |
| `ActiveVoices`, `DroppedVoices` | Voices playing now, and plays dropped because every voice was busy. |
| `Peak` | The loudest sample of the last buffer, before the clip to -1..1. |
| `RenderLoad`, `MaxRenderLoad` | How long the last render took, as a fraction of the time its samples last (0.1 is 10% of the deadline), and the highest since the first quarter second (or since `Audio.ResetMaxRenderLoad()`, which a display showing each second's peak calls once a frame or once a second). Near 1, the output drops out. |
| `DeviceUnderruns` | How many times the output ran out of samples since it opened, as the platform counts them (`IAudioDevice.Underruns`): each is a click or a gap. AAudio counts them (its xruns, carried across a reopen); SDL and the browser don't, and report -1. |

On Android the load reads high for the work done: AAudio runs its callback on a thread the scheduler keeps on a slow,
clocked-down core until the load asks for more, against a deadline of a burst or two (2 ms at 96 frames). A mix that
costs 2% of a core measured offline can read 30% there, with peaks past 50%, and still not drop out: on a Galaxy S23
Ultra, three minutes of a game's busiest play at 30% (peaks to 78%) added no underruns to the ten its start made, while the mix was
compiling and the app loading on every core. The underruns, not the load, say whether it drops out.

---

## 7. Platforms

### The desktop

The desktop host opens the system's default output through SDL 3, at the device's own rate in 32-bit float stereo, and
asks for a 128-frame buffer. SDL rounds it to what the platform's audio API takes: on Windows that is shared-mode
WASAPI's period, 480 frames (10 ms) at 48 kHz. An output on the default device follows the system's default as it
changes (headphones plugged in), which SDL does on its own.

SDL 3 is the same `SDL3.dll` the host reads gamepads with, fetched by `Sdl3.targets` (see
[api-vocabulary.md](api-vocabulary.md#input-on-the-desktop-loomhostingdesktop)). The gamepad pump and the audio device
each start and stop only their own SDL subsystem, so closing one never stops the other. Where SDL3 is missing or won't
load, the app runs silent on a `NullAudioDevice`.

### Android

The Android host opens an AAudio output stream: low-latency performance mode, exclusive sharing where the device
offers it (the MMAP path, straight into the hardware's buffer), usage `GAME`, and a buffer of two bursts, the floor
AAudio's own guidance gives for glitch-free low latency. The mixer renders straight into AAudio's buffer on AAudio's
high-priority callback thread.

- **An exclusive stream can be taken away before it starts.** AAudio reports it disconnected. The device reopens it and
  starts again, and if exclusive use is taken a second time, opens a shared stream instead.
- **When the output changes** (headphones unplugged, a Bluetooth device dropping), AAudio ends the stream. The device
  reopens one on the new output, at the engine's rate, from a thread of its own (AAudio forbids reopening from its
  callbacks). Where the new output won't run at the engine's rate, the app goes silent and logs a warning, since the
  engine's clips were made at the old rate.
- **AAudio calls C# through a native shim.** Android builds `libaaudio` with Control-Flow Integrity, which crashes
  (SIGSEGV in `__cfi_slowpath`) on a callback whose code lies outside any loaded library, and a C#
  `[UnmanagedCallersOnly]` entry point is a runtime stub outside every library. So AAudio calls two forwarding
  functions in `libloomaaudio.so` (`Loom.Hosting.Android/Native/loom_aaudio.c`), built without CFI, and they call the
  C# callbacks. The built libraries for `arm64-v8a` and `x86_64`, linked for 16 KB pages, are checked in under
  `Native/lib/`, so building Loom needs no NDK. Rebuild them with `pwsh Loom.Hosting.Android/Native/build.ps1` after
  changing `loom_aaudio.c`.

### The browser

The .NET runtime can't run on the browser's audio thread, so the browser host turns the usual arrangement around. The
mix runs on the frame thread, once a frame, after the app's tick. It tops up an AudioWorklet's queue to a lead of 50 ms
ahead of the speaker (`AudioOptions.BufferFrames` sets it), and the worklet plays from that queue on the browser's
audio thread. The lead is the web's latency, and it is what rides out a late frame: a frame later than the lead is
heard as a gap.

Because the mix runs on the frame thread, a source's `Render` runs there too. The rules for `Render` and the lock-free
types work the same, so a source written for the desktop runs unchanged.

- **A page makes sound only after the player's first click, tap or key.** The host listens for it and resumes the
  AudioContext. Until then the mix keeps time (voices advance and end) and sends nothing.
- When the frame loop stalls (a background tab), the mix skips the time it missed, a quarter second at most, rather
  than rendering the whole gap at once.
- `__loomAudio()` at the browser's console reports the output's state, its rate and latencies, and the frames sent and
  played (sent minus played is how far the mix runs ahead of the speaker).
- An embedder that boots the .NET runtime itself must register the `loom-audio` JS module beside `loom-webgpu` (see
  `loom-boot.js`).

### A host of your own, and tests

`IHostControl.OpenAudioDevice(AudioOptions)` is how a host hands the app its output. The default returns a
`NullAudioDevice`, so a host with no audio needs nothing. A host with an output implements `IAudioDevice`: once started, it asks the
renderer for interleaved stereo 32-bit float at its `SampleRate`, on a thread of its own (or, as the browser's does,
whenever the host pumps it), and it pauses and resumes on request.

An `AudioEngine` also works on its own, over any `IAudioDevice`. `OfflineAudioDevice` renders only when asked, on the
caller's thread: for tests, for rendering to a file faster than real time, and for a host that pumps audio itself.
`Loom.Audio.Synth`'s `OfflineSession` wraps one, keeping what it renders ([the synthesis guide](synth.md)).
`Loom.Tests` tests the mixer through it (`AudioEngineTests`, `AudioEffectTests`, `AudioDuckTests`, `Audio3DTests`, `AudioStreamTests`, `AudioEventQueueTests`,
`WavDecoderTests`, `VorbisDecoderTests`, `FlacDecoderTests`), and the real
SDL device through `SdlAudioDeviceTests`, which skip where SDL3 or an output is missing.

---

## 8. Not built yet

- Decoders beyond WAV, Ogg Vorbis and FLAC (Opus).
- 3D beyond stereo panning: HRTF (above and behind), occlusion, reverb zones, and sound cones.
- An exclusive-mode WASAPI path below shared mode's 10 ms on Windows.

[`Planning.md` §10](../Planning.md#10-the-audio-track) tracks these.

# Synthesis

What [`Loom.Audio.Synth`](../Loom.Audio.Synth) adds over [the mixer](audio.md): the DSP building blocks a source is
made of, effects for buses, a 16-operator synthesizer chip with patches, samples and drum kits, music written as code
and its sequencer, and sound rendered offline, to measure it in a test or save it as a WAV file to listen to. Beside
it, `Loom.Audio.Workbench` is a window to write the music in (section 10).

The library depends only on `Loom.Audio` and the BCL. The Loom SDK doesn't reference it for an app: an app or test
project that wants it references it itself.

---

## 1. Rendering offline: `OfflineSession`

An `OfflineSession` is an `AudioEngine` over an `OfflineAudioDevice` that keeps what it renders. Nothing renders
until it is asked, and then as fast as the CPU goes, on the calling thread.

```csharp
using var session = new OfflineSession(sampleRate: 48_000);
var music = session.Engine.CreateBus("music");
session.Engine.Play(new MySynth(), music);

session.RenderSeconds(2.0);
float[] left = session.Left();
session.SaveWav("out/synth.wav");
```

- It renders in blocks of at most 256 frames and calls `Engine.Update()` after each, as a host calls it once a frame.
  So a source that finishes is freed in the block it finished in, and an exception a source throws comes out of
  `Render` at the block it was thrown in.
- `Samples` is everything rendered since the session began or since `Clear()`, interleaved stereo. `Clear()` forgets
  it, and the engine plays on from where it was.
- Every call comes from the thread that made the session, as with any `AudioEngine`.
- Two sessions set up the same way render the same bits, so a test may compare renders exactly.

## 2. WAV files: `WavWriter`
